bai.moTa: Change barrier width and compare transmitted counts with theory.
bai.yChinh: Even below the barrier top, a wave can match a nonzero outgoing amplitude on the far side. The transmitted-to-incident flux ratio gives transmission probability.
bai.giaiThich: Monoenergetic electrons strike a one-dimensional square barrier. Both exterior potentials agree. Blue is the stationary scattering density relative to the incident wave; marks on each side sample independent detections.
bai.conSo.1: At E = 2 eV, U = 4 eV and width 0.20 nm, T is about 0.198.
bai.conSo.2: Thick barrier: T ≈ 16E(U − E)/U² · e^(−2κa). With E = 2 eV, U = 4 eV, a = 0.40 nm, the approximation gives 0.0122, the exact value is 0.0121.
bai.hieuDung: Classical momentum has no real value in the barrier at E < U. The wave function remains defined there, and a transmitted electron retains the incident energy.
bai.nguon: Prepared by Trí Lữ. OpenStax, University Physics, Vol. 3, `7.6; Griffiths and Schroeter, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, Ch. 2. NIST CODATA 2022 electron mass, SI h and e.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Predict effects of barrier width and height.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Read the two energies before counting dots. Gold marks the incident energy and the central block the electron potential energy. Both use the same eV scale. Classically kinetic energy is their difference; if negative inside, a particle arriving from the left must turn back before entering.

Slowly lower the top while keeping it above the incident energy. Classical kinetic-energy reasoning gives the same prediction for every barrier width. Keep that prediction for comparison with the wave calculation in the next step.

$$ K=E-U $$

+++ A closer look · The two detectors
Cyan dots at right count transmission and orange dots at left count reflection. Within each tray the spacing only separates marks.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Reset the detectors|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: A wave in a classically forbidden region
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
For E below U the sign in the Schrödinger equation changes inside the barrier. The solution combines two real exponentials, both needed to match both ends of a finite barrier. Blue shows density penetrating the barrier; its vertical scale is separate from eV.

Follow blue from the left face to the right. Density has no jump at the boundary of a finite barrier. Even when a wide barrier makes the far-side value too small to see, the numerical T distinguishes a small signal from zero.

$$ \kappa=\sqrt{2m(U-E)}/\hbar $$

+++ A closer look · Decay length
Inverse κ has units of length. In a thick barrier, going this far reduces the decaying amplitude component by 1/e; its squared magnitude falls faster. With E = 2 eV and U = 4 eV, κ ≈ 7.25 nm⁻¹, so the decay length 1/κ ≈ 0.138 nm, the last entry of the readout.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Choose a thick barrier|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: Why are particles detected beyond it?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
There is only an outgoing wave on the right because illumination is from the left. Matching the wave and its derivative at both faces fixes transmission amplitude. Right-side marks are individual outcomes sampled with probability T. Each electron is detected whole on one side. Rate-limited clicks illustrate transmission events.

The batch button adds independent trials under the same conditions. Repeating it usually gives different counts. Compare the transmitted fraction of all incident particles with theory; an individual dot gives only one outcome.

$$ T=j_{\rm trans}/j_{\rm in}=|t|^2 $$

+++ A closer look · Equal external speeds
The last equality uses equal exterior potentials and hence equal exterior speeds. Unequal potentials require a speed ratio.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Record 100 incident electrons|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Drag the right face away from the left. Height and incident energy stay fixed. The wave now matches across a longer distance before reaching free propagation. Predict which tray receives fewer particles and compare with T. Counts reset when parameters change so that each sample belongs to one setup.

Isolate width by moving only the horizontal handle near the base. Simultaneously raising the top would also reduce counts and obscure the effect of width alone.

$$ T=\left[1+\frac{U^2\sinh^2(\kappa a)}{4E(U-E)}\right]^{-1} $$

+++ A closer look · Check a value
At E = 2 eV, U = 4 eV and a = 0.20 nm, about 19.8% transmit in the many-particle limit. Small groups can differ appreciably.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Reset a to 0.10 nm|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Drag the width until T is within 0.015 of 0.20 at E = 2 eV and U = 4 eV.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: If T is too high, increase the face separation.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Keep width fixed and raise the top. A larger U − E increases the decay constant and shortens the decay length. The blue height on the right drops. Read T and the count and explain why a very small sample can show no transmissions despite positive T.

When the right tray is empty, read theory before concluding transmission is impossible. Wait or add more trials without changing conditions. Separate counters prevent different tray colors from biasing the comparison.

$$ \ell=1/\kappa $$

+++ A closer look · Two ways to reduce T
Both height and width reduce below-barrier transmission, but only height changes κ at fixed E.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Restore U = 4 eV|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Raise the barrier to U − E = 4 eV within 0.12 eV.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Keep E = 2 eV and drag the top handle.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
The static barrier does not absorb. Incident flux divides into reflected and transmitted flux. Left-side density ripples because incident and reflected waves add. A ripple peak may exceed one even though the two outcome probabilities sum to one.

Add the counts and compare the right-hand fraction with T. With many added trials the totals grow while the fraction typically fluctuates less. Conservation constrains total flux without specifying individual outcomes.

$$ R+T=1 $$

+++ A closer look · Density or probability?
Blue is divided by incident-wave density. T and R compare separated fluxes. These normalizations answer different questions.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Record 100 more|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Watch the energy line as width increases. The barrier changes the chance of emerging. A transmitted particle in the same exterior potential has its original kinetic energy. A temporary energy-loan account would mispredict an energy measurement in the outgoing region.

Changing incident energy prepares a different beam. A real source containing several energies may transmit each component differently. The monochromatic source here separates changes in beam composition from changes to one electron’s energy.

$$ E_{\rm out}=E_{\rm in} $$

+++ A closer look · Read the far side
Only a forward wave exists on the right, so stationary density there is flat. Tray dots do not trace paths inside the barrier.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Compare with a wider barrier|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
For a thick barrier a small width change can strongly affect outgoing counts. Predict how to turn frequent transmission into rare events before adjusting. Compare to theoretical T and repeat many trials before judging the observed fraction.

Before reading counts, predict a range of fractions instead of an exact particle count. U and a set transmission probability for the prepared state; each bright dot is a random outcome drawn from it.

> [Ví dụ] With E = 2 eV, U = 4 eV: at a = 0.40 nm (κa ≈ 2.9) the approximation gives T ≈ 0.0122 and the full formula 0.0121, less than 1% apart. At a = 0.10 nm (κa ≈ 0.72) the approximation gives 0.94 while the true value is 0.62: badly wrong. The readout shows both values for comparison.

> [Ví dụ] The scanning tunnelling microscope (STM) relies on exactly this exponential sensitivity. Electrons tunnel across the vacuum gap between the tip and a metal surface; the barrier is about the work function, 4.5 eV, so κ ≈ 10.9 nm⁻¹. Widening the gap by 0.1 nm cuts the current by about 9 times, so the instrument can resolve height changes smaller than an atom.

$$ T\approx\frac{16E(U-E)}{U^2}\,e^{-2\kappa a}\quad(\kappa a\gg1) $$

+++ A closer look · When the approximation holds
The exponential law is the thick-barrier limit. For thin barriers use the full expression so T approaches one correctly.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[Try a thin barrier|thu]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.thuThach.de: At U = 4 eV and E = 2 eV, drag a until T is below 0.02.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.thuThach.goiY: Increase the width to about 0.4 nm.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: Use when κa is well above 1; thin barriers need the full formula.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: For E below U and a finite barrier, what can T be?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: The matched solution has finite transmission.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: What is the energy of a transmitted electron?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: A static potential gives elastic scattering.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: What does T approach as a tends to 0?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Thick barrier (κa ≫ 1). If the width grows by 1/κ, how does T change?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Falls by about a factor e
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: T is proportional to e^(−2κa): adding 1/κ to a lowers the exponent by another 2. Choosing «factor e» confuses the amplitude (down by e) with the probability (amplitude squared).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Why does density ripple on the left?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: A small sample has no transmissions. Does that imply T = 0?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: No. At small positive T a finite run may have no transmissions.
